title: Afghanistan: Kite Fights, Silk Road, and Snow Leopards
summary:
Imagine a country where kids fly kites with wire or glass on the strings—so they can cut their rivals' kite strings in a battle. That's Afghanistan, a country in Central Asia, with Iran to the west and Pakistan to the east. Tall, forbidding mountains and dry deserts cover most of the landscape. The jagged peaks are treacherous and snow-covered for most of the year. Many Afghans live in fertile valleys between the mountains, growing crops and tending animals. Only 20 percent of the land is used as fields. Summers are hot and dry, but winters are very cold, especially north of the Hindu Kush mountains.

Afghanistan is made up of many different groups. About 15 million people—nearly half the population—are Pashtuns, who live in the south around Kandahar. They are descendants of people who came to the country 3,200 years ago. Other groups include Tajiks, who speak Dari; Uzbeks, who speak a language similar to Turkish; and Hazaras, who live in the central mountains and are believed to be descendants of the Mongols. The country was a busy section of the Silk Road, a route merchants traveled over land between China, India, and Europe for over 2,000 years.

Tea is the favorite Afghan drink. A popular meal is palau, made from rice, sheep and goat meats, and fruit. Afghans take pride in making and flying their own kites. They even have kite fights, using wire or glass to cut the kite strings of rival flyers.

Decades of war, hunting, and drought have reduced wildlife. Tigers used to roam the hills, but they are now extinct. Bears and wolves have been hunted nearly to extinction. Endangered snow leopards live in the cold Hindu Kush, relying on their thick fur to stay warm. The country is rich in lapis lazuli, a vibrant blue stone used to decorate the tomb of Egyptian king Tutankhamun.
why_it_matters: A country that usually appears in headlines through conflict is also home to one of the world's oldest trade routes, several distinct ethnic groups and species found nowhere else in the region. Understanding that wider picture makes it much harder to reduce an entire nation to a single story — and it explains why geography so often shapes politics.

background_read: Afghanistan sits at the crossroads of Central and South Asia, which is why it became one of the busiest stretches of the Silk Road — the ancient web of overland routes that carried silk, spices, paper and ideas between China, India, Persia and Europe for centuries.

Goods from Afghan mines travelled the same roads. Lapis lazuli from the northern mountains has been traded for thousands of years and turns up in art far from where it was dug, including in the tomb of Tutankhamun (an Egyptian pharaoh whose burial chamber was discovered in 1922).

The Hindu Kush, the mountain range that runs across the country, has long been both a barrier and a passage. Armies from Alexander the Great to the Mongol empire of Genghis Khan crossed it, and the Hazara people of its central valleys are widely described as descendants of Mongol soldiers.
Kite flying and kite fighting are an old Afghan pastime, made famous to readers around the world by Khaled Hosseini's novel The Kite Runner, which uses a kite competition as a central image.

Wildlife has paid a heavy price for decades of conflict, hunting and drought. Snow leopards survive in the highest, coldest mountains and are listed as a threatened species, while other large animals such as tigers have gone from the country completely.

perspectives.description: Afghanistan's kite-making traditions, its food and tea culture, and its role as a Silk Road crossroads give it a cultural reach far bigger than its size. Its mountains also hold mineral wealth such as lapis lazuli that has been valued abroad for thousands of years.

Decades of war, hunting and drought have stripped the country of much of its wildlife: tigers are gone and bears and wolves have been hunted to the edge. Only a fifth of the land can be farmed, so a growing population depends on a narrow strip of fertile valley.

Afghanistan's position between Iran, Pakistan and Central Asia made it rich in trade and repeatedly invaded, from Alexander the Great to the Mongol empire. The same mountains that made travel treacherous also sheltered distinct peoples, which helps explain why so many languages and groups share one country.

Snow leopards and other remaining species depend on protected high mountain areas, and conservation work across borders is one of the few things neighbouring countries can agree on. Meanwhile, modern road, rail and pipeline projects echo the old Silk Road idea, and the question is whether trade can bring stability without repeating the exploitation of the past.
